The Math We Keep Coming Back To

Different problems, the same mathematical ideas.

The Math We Keep Coming Back To

Four robot quantities

$q\in\R^{7}$joint configuration
$p\in\R^{3}$position
$I\in\R^{3\times H\times W}$image
$a\in\R^{16\times 7}$action chunk

Each is a vector, or an array that can be vectorized.

The Math We Keep Coming Back To

Map

$$f:\R^{n}\to\R^{m},\qquad u\;\mapsto\;y=f(u)$$
domain
$\R^{n}$, the allowed inputs
codomain
$\R^{m}$, the space the outputs live in
u ↦ y
the rule that carries one to the other

The Math We Keep Coming Back To

Local linearisation

$$\boxed{\;f(x+\delta x)\;\approx\;f(x)+J(x)\,\delta x\;}$$
x
the current point
δx
a small change
J(x)
the Jacobian, $J(x)\in\R^{m\times n}$

Many nonlinear robotics problems become linear when viewed locally.

The Math We Keep Coming Back To

Where am I?

$$x_t=f(x_{t-1},u_t)+w_t,\qquad z_t=h(x_t)+v_t$$
xₜ
the latent state, usually not observed directly
uₜ, zₜ
the command, the measurement
f, h
motion and sensor models
wₜ, vₜ
noise

Thrun, S., Burgard, W., Fox, D. Probabilistic Robotics, Ch. 7. MIT Press, 2005.

The Math We Keep Coming Back To

$\|e\|_R^{2}=e\T R^{-1}e$, with $R$ the measurement covariance.

Barfoot, T. D. State Estimation for Robotics, Chapter 4. Cambridge University Press, 2017.

Linear Algebra I

Spaces, Maps, Rank, Solutions

A matrix is a map

$$A\in\R^{m\times n},\qquad x\in\R^{n}\;\longmapsto\;Ax\in\R^{m}$$
A
the map itself, m rows by n columns
x
the input, a column of n numbers
Ax
the output, a column of m numbers
n
input dimension: the number of columns
m
output dimension: the number of rows; m and n need not be equal

Sanderson, G. Essence of Linear Algebra, ch. 3. 3Blue1Brown, 2016.

In numbers

A matrix is a map

$$\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix} =1\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}2+2\\1+2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4\\3\end{bmatrix}$$
$\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}$
the first column, where e₁ lands
$\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}$
the second column, where e₂ lands

A matrix is a map

Linear map

$$\boxed{\,L(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha L(x)+\beta L(y)\,}$$
additivity
$L(x+y)=L(x)+L(y)$, the case $\alpha=\beta=1$
homogeneity
$L(\alpha x)=\alpha L(x)$, the case $\beta=0$
superposition
both at once, for all $x,y$ and all $\alpha,\beta\in\R$

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., Definition 3.1, p. 52. Springer, 2024. Open access.

Questions

Which of these three maps is linear?

A matrix is a map

$$e_j=(0,\ldots,1,\ldots,0)\T$$
the 1
sits in slot j; every other slot holds 0

Column rule

$$\boxed{\,Ae_j=a_j\,}$$
aⱼ
column j of A, a whole output vector

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed.: standard basis 2.27(a), p. 39; columns 3.50, p. 76. Springer, 2024.

A matrix is a map

Linear combination of columns

$$Ax=\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j\,(Ae_j)=x_1a_1+\cdots+x_na_n$$
xⱼ
coordinate j of x, used as an amount
Aeⱼ
column j, from the page before
aⱼ
column j of A, a whole direction

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.50 linear combination of columns, p. 76. Springer, 2024.

A matrix is a map

$$\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\2&1&3\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}3\\2\\0\end{bmatrix}=3a_1+2a_2=\begin{bmatrix}3\\2\\8\end{bmatrix}$$
a₁, a₂
(1,0,2) and (0,1,1), the first two columns
3, 2, 0
the amounts asked of the three columns

A matrix is a map

Do B first, then A

$$(AB)x=A(Bx)$$
shapes
$B\in\R^{n\times p}$, $A\in\R^{m\times n}$
Bx
where B sends x first
A(Bx)
where A then sends that

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.43 matrix of product of linear maps, p. 74. Springer, 2024.

A matrix is a map

Transpose

$$(A\T)_{k,j}=A_{j,k}$$
row j
of A becomes column j of Aᵀ
m × n
becomes n × m

It reverses a product

$$\boxed{\,(AB)\T=B\T A\T\,}$$
(AB)ᵀ
p × m, the shape the answer must have
BᵀAᵀ
p × n times n × m, so n meets n

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.54 transpose, p. 77; (AC)ᵗ = CᵗAᵗ, p. 78. Springer, 2024.

v_i

c_i

w

Span

$$\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_k)=\{c_1v_1+\cdots+c_kv_k\;:\;c_i\in\R\}$$
{ }
every w the weights can reach, all at once

Worked example

$v_1=(1,0,2)$, $v_2=(0,1,1)$: $3v_1+2v_2=(3,2,8)$ is in the span.

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 2.4 span, p. 29. Springer, 2024.

Span and column space

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname{span}(v_1)&=\{c\,v_1\}\\ \operatorname{span}(v_1,v_2)&=\{c_1v_1+c_2v_2\}\\ \operatorname{span}(v_1,v_2,v_3)&=\operatorname{span}(v_1,v_2) \end{aligned}$$
the conditions
zero spans only $\{0\}$; a dependent pair spans a line
v₃
already a mixture of the first two

Sanderson, G. Essence of Linear Algebra, Chapter 2. 3Blue1Brown, 2016.

A =
1 0 1
0 1 1
2 1 3
$$b\in\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_k)\iff Vc=b\ \text{has a solution}$$
V
the arrows as columns
c
the unknown weights
b
the target vector

Is (3,2,9) in the span?

$c_1(1,0,2)+c_2(0,1,1)=(3,2,9)$

row 1 gives $c_1=3$, row 2 gives $c_2=2$

row 3 is then forced: $2(3)+2=8$, not 9

Span and column space

A vector space is a set equipped with vector addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms.

What we use

$$\boxed{\,u,v\in V,\ \alpha,\beta\in\R\ \Longrightarrow\ \alpha u+\beta v\in V\,}$$
closure
the one property this course leans on all term

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 1.20 vector space, p. 12. Springer, 2024.

Span and column space

Addition

$$\boxed{\begin{aligned}u+v&=v+u & (u+v)+w&=u+(v+w)\\ v+0&=v & \exists\,w:\ v+w&=0\end{aligned}}$$
0 and $w$
an origin, and an undo for every vector

Scaling

$$\boxed{\begin{aligned}1v&=v & \alpha(\beta v)&=(\alpha\beta)v\\ \alpha(u+v)&=\alpha u+\alpha v & (\alpha+\beta)v&=\alpha v+\beta v\end{aligned}}$$
the payoff
obey all eight and every theorem here applies

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 1.20 vector space, p. 12. Springer, 2024.

Span and column space

A subset $S\subseteq V$ is a subspace if it is itself a vector space under the same operations.

Equivalent test

$$\boxed{\,S\neq\varnothing\ \ \text{and}\ \ u,v\in S,\ \alpha,\beta\in\R\Rightarrow\alpha u+\beta v\in S\,}$$
nonempty
plus closure already gives $0\in S$: choose $\alpha=\beta=0$
next page
the same test, split into three checks

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 1.33 subspace and 1.34 conditions for a subspace, p. 18. Springer, 2024.

Span and column space

Conditions for a subspace

$$0\in S;\qquad u+v\in S;\qquad \alpha u\in S$$
0
the zero vector is a member
u+v
any two members add to a member
alpha u
any multiple stays in, negatives included

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 1.34 conditions for a subspace, p. 18. Springer, 2024.

Span and column space

Fastest disqualifier

$$0\notin S\ \Longrightarrow\ S\ \text{is not a subspace}$$
0 ∈ S
necessary, never sufficient: closure still has to hold

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 1.35 example: subspaces, p. 19. Springer, 2024.

Span and column space

Claim

$$\boxed{\,v_1,\dots,v_k\in V\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_k)\ \text{is a subspace of}\ V\,}$$
S
every mixture of the list; the smallest subspace containing it
$$0=\sum_{i=1}^{k}0\,v_i\in S$$
every ci = 0
the origin is a member
$$\alpha u+\beta w=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(\alpha c_i+\beta d_i)\,v_i\in S$$
u, w
any two members: $u=\sum_i c_iv_i$, $w=\sum_i d_iv_i$

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 2.6 span is the smallest containing subspace, p. 29. Springer, 2024.

Span and column space

Column space

$$\boxed{\,\mathcal{C}(A)=\{Ax:x\in\R^{n}\}\subseteq\R^{m}\,}$$
A
any $m\times n$ matrix; x runs over the whole of $\R^{n}$
$\subseteq\R^{m}$
a subspace of the codomain; if $m=n$ the roles still differ
also called
the image of A, or the range of A

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.16 range and 3.18 the range is a subspace, p. 61. Springer, 2024.

Span and column space

Definition

$$\mathcal{C}(A)=\{Ax:x\in\R^{n}\}$$
x
runs over every input

Column view

$$Ax=\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j\,a_j$$
aj
column j of A

⇓

$$\boxed{\,\mathcal{C}(A)=\operatorname{span}(a_1,\dots,a_n)\,}$$
one set
reachable outputs and mixtures of the columns are the same thing

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.16 range, p. 61; 3.50 linear combination of columns, p. 76. Springer, 2024.

Span and column space

Question

$$Ax=b\ ?$$
b
a target on the output side
$$Ax=b\ \text{has a solution}\iff\exists\,x:\ Ax=b\iff b\in\{Ax:x\in\R^{n}\}$$
∃ x
the whole question is whether one input reaches b
$$\boxed{\,Ax=b\ \text{is solvable}\iff b\in\mathcal{C}(A)\,}$$
nothing new
the right side is the definition of C(A), read backwards

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.16 range, p. 61. Springer, 2024.

Span and column space

Solve

$$c_1\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{bmatrix}+c_2\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\\2\\y_3\end{bmatrix}$$
row 1
$c_1+0=3$, so $c_1=3$
row 2
$0+c_2=2$, so $c_2=2$
row 3
$2c_1+c_2=2(3)+2=8$ must equal $y_3$

Target 1

$$\boxed{\,y_3=8:\ 8=8\ \checkmark\,}$$
so
$b_1=3a_1+2a_2\in\mathcal{C}(A)$

Target 2

$$\boxed{\,y_3=9:\ 9\neq8\ \times\,}$$
so
no $c$ works: $b_2\notin\mathcal{C}(A)$

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.16 range, p. 61. Springer, 2024.

A =
1 0 1
0 1 1
2 1 3
$$\boxed{\,Ax=\sum_{j}x_j\,a_j\,}$$
xj
the amount taken of column j

⇓

$$\boxed{\,\mathcal{C}(A)=\operatorname{span}(a_1,\dots,a_n)\,}$$
span
every mixture, so every reachable output

⇓

$$\boxed{\,Ax=b\ \text{solvable}\iff b\in\mathcal{C}(A)\,}$$
our A
$a_3=a_1+a_2$, so the third column adds nothing to the span

When do different columns carry independent information?

Null Space and Linear Independence

Null Space and Linear Independence

So far

$$\mathcal{C}(A)=\text{all reachable outputs}$$
settled
which targets can be hit, and by which mixtures

Now ask

$$\boxed{\,Ax_1=Ax_2,\qquad x_1\neq x_2\,}$$
one output
but more than one input that reaches it

How can two different inputs produce the same output?

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.14 injective, p. 60; 3.11 null space, p. 59. Springer, 2024.

Null Space and Linear Independence

$$\begin{aligned} Ax_1&=Ax_2\\ Ax_1-Ax_2&=0\\ A(x_1-x_2)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
last step
linearity, and nothing else, is what pulls A outside

The difference

$$\boxed{\,z=x_1-x_2\ \Longrightarrow\ Az=0\,}$$
z
nonzero, since $x_1\neq x_2$, and A sends it to zero

Every collision $Ax_1=Ax_2$ is a solution $z=x_1-x_2$ of $Ax=0$.

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.1 linear map, p. 52; 3.11 null space, p. 59. Springer, 2024.

Null Space and Linear Independence

Homogeneous system

$$\boxed{\,Ax=0\,}$$
homogeneous
the right-hand side is the zero vector
x = 0
always a solution, and the uninteresting one

Are there nonzero solutions?

One gives a line

$$\boxed{\,Az=0,\ z\neq0\ \Longrightarrow\ A(\alpha z)=0\ \ \forall\,\alpha\in\R\,}$$
αz
one invisible direction, so a whole line of invisible inputs

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.26 homogeneous system of linear equations, p. 65. Springer, 2024.

Null Space and Linear Independence

Null space

$$\boxed{\,\N(A)=\{x\in\R^{n}:Ax=0\}\,}$$
also called
the kernel of A, written $\ker(A)$
$Ax=0$
the inputs A cannot see

Shape

$$\boxed{\,\N(A)\subseteq\R^{n}\,}\qquad\text{against}\qquad\mathcal{C}(A)\subseteq\R^{m}$$
input side
N(A) lives where x lives, C(A) where Ax lives

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.11 null space and 3.13 the null space is a subspace, p. 59. Springer, 2024.

Null Space and Linear Independence

$$u,v\in\N(A)\ \Longrightarrow\ Au=0,\ Av=0$$
and
$A0=0$, so the origin is in $\N(A)$ to begin with
$$A(\alpha u+\beta v)=\alpha Au+\beta Av=0$$
so
$\alpha u+\beta v\in\N(A)$ for every $\alpha,\beta$

Subspace

$$\boxed{\,\N(A)\ \text{is a subspace of}\ \R^{n}\,}$$
flat
in this $\R^{3}$ example: a point, a line, or a plane through 0

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.13 the null space is a subspace, p. 59. Springer, 2024.

0 1 1
2 1 3

Our matrix

$$a_3=a_1+a_2\ \Longrightarrow\ a_1+a_2-a_3=0$$
read it
a mixture of the columns, weights $1,1,-1$, giving zero
$$A\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\-1\end{bmatrix}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\-1\end{bmatrix}\in\N(A)$$
and
the next page solves for all of it

The whole set

$$\boxed{\,\N(A)=\operatorname{span}\left\{(1,1,-1)\T\right\}\,}$$
a line
through the origin

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.11 null space, p. 59. Springer, 2024.

Null Space and Linear Independence

Ax = 0

$$\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\2&1&3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{bmatrix}=0$$
row 1
$1x_1+0x_2+1x_3=0$, so $x_1+x_3=0$
row 2
$0x_1+1x_2+1x_3=0$
row 3
$2x_1+x_2+3x_3=0$ is twice row 1 plus row 2

Solve

$$x_3=t:\ x_1=-t,\ x_2=-t,\ x=t(-1,-1,1)\T$$
why
one free unknown

Null space

$$\boxed{\,\N(A)=\operatorname{span}\{(-1,-1,1)\T\}\,}$$
check
$-1+1,\ -1+1,\ -2-1+3$: all zero

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.11 null space, p. 59. Springer, 2024.

Null Space and Linear Independence

$$z\in\N(A)\ \Longrightarrow\ Az=0\ \Longrightarrow\ A(x+z)=Ax+Az=Ax$$
x
any input at all, not a special one

What it means

$$\boxed{\,A(x+z)=Ax,\qquad z\in\N(A)\,}$$
x + z
a whole line of inputs, all landing on one output

Null-space directions are invisible to the map.

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.1 linear map, p. 52; 3.11 null space, p. 59. Springer, 2024.

Null Space and Linear Independence

On a robot

$$\dot x=J(q)\,\dot q$$
$\dot q$
joint velocities, what you command
$\dot x$
end-effector velocity, what the world sees

Redundancy

$$\boxed{\,z\in\N(J(q))\ \Longrightarrow\ J(q)(\dot q+z)=J(q)\dot q\,}$$
z
a joint-velocity direction that produces no end-effector velocity

Lynch, K. M. and Park, F. C. Modern Robotics, §6.3 inverse velocity kinematics, p. 233. Cambridge University Press, 2017 preprint.

Null Space and Linear Independence

Linear independence

$$\boxed{\,c_1v_1+\cdots+c_kv_k=0\ \Longrightarrow\ c_1=\cdots=c_k=0\,}$$
read it
the all-zero weights are the only ones that cancel

Same thing

$$\boxed{\,\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_iv_i=0\ \Longrightarrow\ c=0\,}$$
c
the whole list of weights, read as one vector

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 2.15 linearly independent, p. 32. Springer, 2024.

Null Space and Linear Independence

Linear dependence

$$\boxed{\,\exists\,c\neq0:\ c_1v_1+\cdots+c_kv_k=0\,}$$
$c\neq0$
at least one weight is nonzero; say it is $c_j$

Solve for that one

$$\boxed{\,v_j=-\frac{1}{c_j}\sum_{i\neq j}c_iv_i\,}$$
so
$v_j$ is built from the others, and deleting it leaves the span unchanged

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 2.17 linearly dependent and 2.19 linear dependence lemma, p. 33. Springer, 2024.

Null Space and Linear Independence

Stack them

$$V=[\,v_1\ \cdots\ v_k\,],\qquad Vc=\sum_i c_iv_i$$
Vc
the mixture, written as a matrix times its weights

The anchor

$$\boxed{\begin{aligned}v_1,\dots,v_k\ \text{independent}&\iff\N(V)=\{0\}\\v_1,\dots,v_k\ \text{dependent}&\iff\N(V)\neq\{0\}\end{aligned}}$$
one question
redundancy in a list is a null space

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 2.15 linearly independent, p. 32; 3.15 injectivity, p. 60. Springer, 2024.

the chain
definition, meaning, cost

A =
1 0 1
0 1 1
2 1 3

We know

$$\mathcal{C}(A)\ \text{what A can produce},\qquad \N(A)\ \text{what A cannot see}$$
and
how to tell whether a direction is redundant

Now ask

our A

Basis, Dimension, and Rank

Basis

$$\boxed{\,\text{Basis}=\text{Spanning}+\text{Linear Independence}\,}$$
spans
$\operatorname{span}(b_1,\dots,b_k)=V$
independent
$c_1b_1+\cdots+c_kb_k=0\Rightarrow c_1=\cdots=c_k=0$

So

$$\text{enough to build everything, with nothing spare}$$
both halves
either one alone is not a basis

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 2.26 basis, p. 39. Springer, 2024.

Basis, Dimension, and Rank

Basis

$$\boxed{\,\text{enough, but not too many}\,}$$
too few
here independent, but does not reach everything
too many
reaches everything, but carries a repeat

Worked example

In $\R^{2}$: $\{(1,0)\}$ is too few, $\{(1,0),(1,1)\}$ is a basis, adding $(2,1)$ is too many.

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 2.26 basis, p. 39. Springer, 2024.

Basis, Dimension, and Rank

Unique weights

$$x=c_1b_1+\cdots+c_kb_k\ \text{in exactly one way}$$
why
independence: two different weightings would differ by a nonzero mix that vanishes

Coordinates

$$\boxed{\,[x]_B=(c_1,\dots,c_k)\T,\qquad x=B\,[x]_B\,}$$
one address
the vector does not change; only its coordinates do

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 2.28 criterion for basis, p. 39; 3.73 matrix of a vector, p. 88. Springer, 2024.

Basis, Dimension, and Rank

Dimension

$$\boxed{\,\dim V=\text{the number of vectors in any basis of }V\,}$$
any
every basis of the same space has the same length

Reading

$$\text{dimension counts independent degrees of freedom}$$
finite
every space in this course has a finite basis
$$\boxed{\,\dim\{0\}=0\,}$$
zero space
the empty list is a basis of it

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 2.35 dimension, p. 44. Springer, 2024.

A =

2 1 3

Same size always

$$\boxed{\,\text{different bases, different arrows, the same number of them}\,}$$
this plane
every basis of it has exactly two vectors
so
dimension belongs to the space, not to a choice

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 2.35 dimension, p. 44. Springer, 2024.

Reduce

$$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\2&1&3\end{bmatrix}\xrightarrow{r_3\leftarrow r_3-2r_1}\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}\xrightarrow{r_3\leftarrow r_3-r_2}\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}=R$$
step 1
$(2,1,3)-2(1,0,1)=(0,1,1)$
step 2
$(0,1,1)-(0,1,1)=(0,0,0)$
pivots
columns 1 and 2

Why R

$$R=EA,\ E\ \text{invertible}:\ Ax=0\iff Rx=0$$
so
$\N(A)=\N(R)$

Strang, G. 18.06, Lecture 7: pivot variables and special solutions. MIT OCW, 2010.

Basis, Dimension, and Rank

Pivot

$$\boxed{\,\text{the leading nonzero entry of a nonzero row of }R\,}$$
in R
pivot positions are read off the echelon form, not off $A$
pivot variable
a variable whose column carries a pivot
free variable
a variable whose column does not

Here

$$x_1,x_2\ \text{pivot};\qquad x_3\ \text{free}$$
count
3 variables, 2 pivots, 1 free

Strang, G. 18.06, Lecture 7: pivot variables and special solutions. MIT OCW, 2010.

Basis, Dimension, and Rank

Pivot columns

$$\boxed{\,\text{the pivot columns of }A\ \text{are a basis for }\mathcal{C}(A)\,}$$
but
$\N(A)=\N(R)$, while $\mathcal{C}(A)\neq\mathcal{C}(R)$
R's columns
$(1,0,0)\T,(0,1,0)\T$ span $y_3=0$; $a_1=(1,0,2)\T$ has $y_3=2$
A's columns
$a_1,a_2$ independent, and $a_3=a_1+a_2$, so they span $\mathcal{C}(A)$

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.52 column rank, p. 77. Springer, 2024.

Basis, Dimension, and Rank

A =
1 0 1
0 1 1
2 1 3
R =
1 0 1
0 1 1
0 0 0

Rows of R

$$x_1+x_3=0,\qquad x_2+x_3=0,\qquad 0=0$$
legal
$\N(A)=\N(R)$
free
column 3 has no pivot: $x_3=t$

Solve

$$x_1=-t,\quad x_2=-t\ \Longrightarrow\ x=(-t,-t,t)\T=t(-1,-1,1)\T$$
$t=1$
on $A$: $-1+1,\ -1+1,\ -2-1+3$, all zero

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.11 null space, p. 59. Springer, 2024.

Basis, Dimension, and Rank

All solutions

$$\N(A)=\{\,t(-1,-1,1)\T:\ t\in\R\,\}$$
why
every solution is $t$ times one vector, nothing else
so
all multiples of one vector: a span

Basis and dimension

$$\boxed{\,\N(A)=\operatorname{span}\{(-1,-1,1)\T\},\qquad\dim\N(A)=1\,}$$
basis
one nonzero vector is independent on its own, so it is a basis
count
one free variable, one basis vector: $\dim\N(A)=$ free variables

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.11 null space, p. 59; 2.26 basis, p. 39. Springer, 2024.

Basis, Dimension, and Rank

A =
1 0 1
0 1 1
2 1 3

Rank

$$\boxed{\,\operatorname{rank}(A)=\dim\mathcal{C}(A)\,}$$
our A
$\dim\mathcal{C}(A)=2$, so $\operatorname{rank}(A)=2$

To compute

$$\boxed{\,\operatorname{rank}(A)=\text{the number of pivots}\,}$$
reading
how many independent output directions A can produce

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.58 rank, p. 79; 3.52 column rank, p. 77. Springer, 2024.

Basis, Dimension, and Rank

Into three-space

$$r=3\ \text{volume};\quad r=2\ \text{plane};\quad r=1\ \text{line};\quad r=0\ \text{the point }\{0\}$$
rank
the dimension of the reachable output space

Sanderson, G. Essence of Linear Algebra, ch. 7. 3Blue1Brown, 2016.

Basis, Dimension, and Rank

A =
1 0 1
0 1 1
2 1 3

Nullity

$$\boxed{\,\operatorname{nullity}(A)=\dim\N(A)\,}$$
our A
$\N(A)=\operatorname{span}\{(-1,-1,1)\T\}$, so $\operatorname{nullity}(A)=1$

Reading

$$\text{independent input directions lost by }A$$
the pair
rank counts what survives, nullity counts what disappears

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.11 null space, p. 59. Springer, 2024.

Basis, Dimension, and Rank

A =
1 0 1
0 1 1
2 1 3

Rank–nullity

$$\boxed{\,\operatorname{rank}(A)+\operatorname{nullity}(A)=n\,}$$
n
the number of columns, the input dimension
reach
$\dim\mathcal{C}(A)=r$: directions that survive
loss
$\dim\N(A)=n-r$: directions that disappear
our A
$2+1=3$
a choice
$n-r$ basis vectors in $\N(A)$, $r$ whose images span $\mathcal{C}(A)$

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.21 fundamental theorem of linear maps, p. 62. Springer, 2024.

Basis, Dimension, and Rank

The map

$$A:\R^{n}\to\R^{m},\qquad n=r+(n-r)$$
r
directions that survive
n - r
directions that vanish

So

$$\boxed{\,\text{rank--nullity counts the input side}\,}$$
not m
the null space is not in the output space

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.21 fundamental theorem of linear maps, p. 62. Springer, 2024.

Basis, Dimension, and Rank

Exam question

$$B\in\R^{7\times10},\qquad \operatorname{rank}(B)=6$$
ask
$\dim\mathcal{C}(B)$, $\dim\N(B)$, and the number of free variables
$$\dim\mathcal{C}(B)=6,\qquad \dim\N(B)=10-6=4,\qquad \text{4 free variables}$$
the trap
use the 10, not the 7

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.21 fundamental theorem of linear maps, p. 62. Springer, 2024.

Basis, Dimension, and Rank

Full column rank

$$\boxed{\,r=n\,}$$
then
$\N(A)=\{0\}$: no input direction is lost; needs $n\le m$

Full row rank

$$\boxed{\,r=m\,}$$
then
$\mathcal{C}(A)=\R^{m}$: every output is reachable; needs $m\le n$

One is about losing nothing. The other is about reaching everything.

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.21 fundamental theorem of linear maps, p. 62. Springer, 2024.

Basis, Dimension, and Rank

Where we are

$$\dim\mathcal{C}(A)=r,\qquad \dim\N(A)=n-r$$
so
the three questions become countable
$$\begin{aligned} \text{is }b\text{ reachable?}&\quad b\in\mathcal{C}(A)\\ \text{is }x\text{ unique?}&\quad \N(A)=\{0\}\\ \text{how many free directions?}&\quad n-r \end{aligned}$$
row two
uniqueness is a question only once a solution exists

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.21 fundamental theorem of linear maps, p. 62. Springer, 2024.

Linear Systems and Solution Sets

Linear Systems and Solution Sets

Return to

$$\boxed{\,Ax=b\,}$$
1 existence
does a solution exist?
2 uniqueness
if it exists, is it the only one?
3 structure
what are all of them?

With

$$\mathcal{C}(A)\quad\text{and}\quad\N(A)$$
nothing new
both spaces are already built and measured

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.16 range, p. 61; 3.11 null space, p. 59. Springer, 2024.

Linear Systems and Solution Sets

Solution set

$$\boxed{\,\mathcal{S}(A,b)=\{x\in\R^{n}:Ax=b\}\,}$$
a solution
any x that produces the requested b
consistent
$\mathcal{S}(A,b)\neq\emptyset$; otherwise inconsistent

Three possibilities

$$\text{empty},\qquad \text{one point},\qquad \text{infinitely many}$$
never two
two solutions force infinitely many: a line, a plane, or higher

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.11 null space, p. 59. Springer, 2024.

Linear Systems and Solution Sets

A =
1 0 1
0 1 1
2 1 3

Recall

$$\mathcal{C}(A)=\{Ax:x\in\R^{n}\}$$
so
b is reachable exactly when some x reaches it

Existence

$$\boxed{\,Ax=b\ \text{is consistent}\iff b\in\mathcal{C}(A)\,}$$
one sentence
the column space controls existence

Worked example

$\mathcal{C}(A)$ is $y_3=2y_1+y_2$: $(3,2,8)$ passes since $2(3)+2=8$; $(3,2,9)$ fails.

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.16 range, p. 61. Springer, 2024.

Linear Systems and Solution Sets

Suppose

$$Ax_1=b,\quad Ax_2=b\ \Longrightarrow\ A(x_1-x_2)=0\ \Longrightarrow\ x_1-x_2\in\N(A)$$
so
if $\N(A)=\{0\}$ then $x_1=x_2$

Uniqueness

$$\boxed{\,\N(A)=\{0\}\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{at most one solution}\,}$$
careful
at most one, not one
if consistent
then it means exactly one

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.15 injectivity, p. 60. Springer, 2024.

Linear Systems and Solution Sets

Particular

$$\boxed{\,Ax_p=b\ \text{for one particular }x_p\,}$$
any one
it does not matter which solution you found

General

$$\boxed{\,\mathcal{S}(A,b)=x_p+\N(A)=\{x_p+z:z\in\N(A)\}\,}$$
recipe
find one solution, then add everything A ignores

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.11 null space, p. 59. Springer, 2024.

Linear Systems and Solution Sets

Each one works

$$A(x_p+z)=b+0=b$$
uses
linearity and $Az=0$

Nothing is missed

$$Ax=b\Rightarrow A(x-x_p)=0$$
so
$x=x_p+z$ with $z=x-x_p\in\N(A)$

Equality

$$\boxed{\,\mathcal{S}(A,b)=x_p+\N(A)\,}$$
both ways
one inclusion each, which is what an equality of sets needs

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.11 null space, p. 59. Springer, 2024.

Linear Systems and Solution Sets

Augment

$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&0&1&3\\0&1&1&2\\2&1&3&8\end{array}\right]\xrightarrow{r_3\leftarrow r_3-2r_1}\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&0&1&3\\0&1&1&2\\0&1&1&2\end{array}\right]\xrightarrow{r_3\leftarrow r_3-r_2}\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&0&1&3\\0&1&1&2\\0&0&0&0\end{array}\right]$$
step 1
$(2,1,3|8)-2(1,0,1|3)=(0,1,1|2)$
step 2
$(0,1,1|2)-(0,1,1|2)=(0,0,0|0)$
row 3
$0=0$: consistent

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.11 null space, p. 59. Springer, 2024.

Linear Systems and Solution Sets

Read off

$$x_1+x_3=3,\quad x_2+x_3=2,\quad x_3=t\ \Longrightarrow\ x_1=3-t,\ x_2=2-t$$
free
no pivot in column 3: choose $x_3$
$t=0$
one particular solution, $x_p=(3,2,0)\T$

All of them

$$\boxed{\,x=(3,2,0)\T+t\,(-1,-1,1)\T,\qquad t\in\R\,}$$
$t=1$
$(2,1,1)\T$: $2+1=3$, $1+1=2$, $4+1+3=8$
$b=(3,2,9)\T$
same steps: $9-6=3$, $3-2=1$, so row 3 reads $0=1$: no solution

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.11 null space, p. 59. Springer, 2024.

Linear Systems and Solution Sets

Affine set

$$\boxed{\,x_0+S=\{x_0+s:s\in S\}\ \text{for a subspace }S\,}$$
here
$\mathcal{S}(A,b)=x_p+\N(A)$: the null space, translated
through 0?
only if $b=0$; then $\mathcal{S}=\N(A)$, a subspace

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 1.34 conditions for a subspace, p. 18. Springer, 2024.

Linear Systems and Solution Sets

Notation

$$r=\operatorname{rank}(A)$$
unique
when consistent, means $r=n$

Cases

$$\boxed{\begin{aligned}b\notin\mathcal{C}(A)&:\ \text{none}\\b\in\mathcal{C}(A),\ \N(A)=\{0\}&:\ \text{one}\\b\in\mathcal{C}(A),\ \dim\N(A)>0&:\ \text{infinitely many}\end{aligned}}$$
free
$n-r$ directions

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.21 fundamental theorem of linear maps, p. 62. Springer, 2024.

Invertibility and Singular Matrices

Invertibility and Singular Matrices

Demand

$$\mathcal{C}(A)=\R^{m}\ \text{and}\ \N(A)=\{0\}$$
reach
$r=m$: nothing is missed
no loss
$r=n$ by rank--nullity

So

$$\boxed{\,m=n\ \text{and}\ r=n\,}$$
square
a conclusion, not a hypothesis

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.21 fundamental theorem of linear maps, p. 62. Springer, 2024.

Invertibility and Singular Matrices

Inverse

$$\boxed{\,AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I\,}$$
shapes
$A,A^{-1}\in\R^{n\times n}$ and $I=I_n$
both sides
two-sided by definition; for square $A$ either half implies the other

Singular

$$\boxed{\,A\ \text{singular}\iff A\ \text{has no inverse}\,}$$
nonsingular
the same word

Worked example

$\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}$

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.79 identity, p. 90; 3.80 invertible and the word singular, p. 91; 3.60 inverse is unique, p. 82. Springer, 2024.

Invertibility and Singular Matrices

In general

$$A\ \text{invertible}\iff A\ \text{injective and surjective}$$
injective
$Ax=Ay\Rightarrow x=y$
surjective
$\mathcal{C}(A)=\R^{m}$

If A is square

$$\boxed{\,\N(A)=\{0\}\iff \mathcal{C}(A)=\R^{n}\iff A\ \text{invertible}\,}$$
saving
check one side, the other follows
why
rank--nullity: $r=n$ makes both true at once

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.63 invertibility, p. 83; 3.65 injectivity equivalent to surjectivity, p. 84. Springer, 2024.

Invertibility and Singular Matrices

Square A

$$\boxed{\begin{aligned}A\ \text{invertible}&\iff r=n\iff\N(A)=\{0\}\\&\iff\text{columns independent}\iff\mathcal{C}(A)=\R^{n}\end{aligned}}$$
and
$\iff Ax=b$ has one solution for every $b$
det
a preview; the determinant is a later module

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.63 invertibility, p. 83; 3.65, p. 84; 3.21, p. 62. Springer, 2024.

Invertibility and Singular Matrices

Singular

$$\boxed{\,\N(B)\neq\{0\}\iff B\ \text{singular}\,}$$
B
square and rank deficient

Worked example

$B=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}$ has $r=1$, and $B(2,-1)\T=0$: a nonzero input lands on zero.

Sanderson, G. Essence of Linear Algebra, ch. 7. 3Blue1Brown, 2016 · Axler, 4th ed., 3.80, p. 91.

Invertibility and Singular Matrices

Preview · least squares

$$X=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\\3&6\end{bmatrix},\qquad X\T X=\begin{bmatrix}1+4+9&2+8+18\\2+8+18&4+16+36\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}14&28\\28&56\end{bmatrix}$$
the fit
$\min_\beta\|X\beta-y\|^{2}\ \Rightarrow\ X\T X\beta=X\T y$
entries
$(X\T X)_{ij}$ is column $i$ dotted with column $j$; the off-diagonal pair agree

Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y. and Courville, A. Deep Learning, ch. 2. MIT Press, 2016.

Invertibility and Singular Matrices

Singular

$$X\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2-2\\4-4\\6-6\end{bmatrix}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ X\T X\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\end{bmatrix}=0$$
collinear
column 2 is twice column 1: $(2,-1)\T\in\N(X)$

Null spaces

$$\boxed{\,X\T Xz=0\ \Rightarrow\ \|Xz\|^{2}=z\T X\T Xz=0\ \Rightarrow\ Xz=0\,}$$
so
$\N(X\T X)=\N(X)$
the fit
$\beta+t(2,-1)\T$ gives the same $X\beta$: not identifiable

Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y. and Courville, A. Deep Learning, ch. 2. MIT Press, 2016.

Invertibility and Singular Matrices

At a singularity

$$\boxed{\,J(q)\ \text{loses rank}\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{a tool direction is lost}\,}$$
rank drop
$\mathcal{C}(J)$ shrinks: some $\dot x$ has no $\dot q$
nearby
joint rates grow without bound for tool directions along the lost one

Next

$$\mathcal{C}(A),\ \N(A),\ \mathcal{C}(A\T),\ \N(A\T)$$
one matrix
four spaces, one rank

Lynch, K. M. and Park, F. C. Modern Robotics, §5.3 singularity analysis, p. 191. Cambridge University Press, 2017 preprint.

The Four Fundamental Subspaces

The Four Fundamental Subspaces

So far

$$A:\R^{n}\to\R^{m},\qquad \mathcal{C}(A)\ \text{and}\ \N(A)$$
but
$A\T:\R^{m}\to\R^{n}$ is a linear map too

So ask

$$\boxed{\,\text{what spaces come from }A\T?\,}$$
the answer
$\mathcal{C}(A\T)$ and $\N(A\T)$: two more, for free

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.54 transpose, p. 77. Springer, 2024.

The Four Fundamental Subspaces

New names

$$\boxed{\,\operatorname{Row}(A)=\mathcal{C}(A\T),\qquad \N(A\T)=\{y:A\T y=0\}\,}$$
left null
$A\T y=0$ is $y\T A=0\T$: y multiplies from the left

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.54 transpose, p. 77; 3.11 null space, p. 59. Springer, 2024.

The Four Fundamental Subspaces

Output side

$$\mathcal{C}(A)=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,2)\T,(0,1,1)\T\}$$
$\N(A\T)$
$=\operatorname{span}\{(-2,-1,1)\T\}$

Input side

$$\operatorname{Row}(A)=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,1)\T,(0,1,1)\T\}$$
$\N(A)$
$=\operatorname{span}\{(-1,-1,1)\T\}$

So

$$\boxed{\,y=(-2,-1,1)\T,\qquad A\T y=0\,}$$
read it
the row weights

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.57 column rank equals row rank, p. 78. Springer, 2024.

The Four Fundamental Subspaces

Rank equality

$$\boxed{\,\operatorname{rank}(A)=\operatorname{rank}(A\T)=r\,}$$
so
column rank equals row rank

All four

$$\boxed{\begin{aligned}\dim\mathcal{C}(A)&=r&\dim\N(A)&=n-r\\\dim\mathcal{C}(A\T)&=r&\dim\N(A\T)&=m-r\end{aligned}}$$
two sums
$r+(n-r)=n$ and $r+(m-r)=m$

Worked example

Our $A$: $r=2$, so $2+1=3$ columns and $2+1=3$ rows.

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.57 column rank equals row rank, p. 78; 3.21, p. 62. Springer, 2024.

The Four Fundamental Subspaces

M1 in one line

$$\boxed{\,\dim=r,\ n-r,\ r,\ m-r\,}$$
later
the two pairs form orthogonal-complement decompositions

Axler, S. Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., 3.21, p. 62; 3.57, p. 78. Springer, 2024.
